newsitem.title: UK: China sees "green" light in new light bulbs.
newsitem.headline: China sees "green" light in new light bulbs.

text.p: China could reduce its lighting electricity use by 25 percent by the year 2,000 simply by changing light bulbs, a report said.

In its March quarterly newsletter, the International Institute for Energy Conservation (IIEC) said China had launched the Green Lights programme -- a campaign to dramatically cut lighting electricity demand.
Lighting accounts for 13 percent of the country's total electricity use, according to official data.
The program projects China can cut some 24 Tera Watt hours of electricity usage by introducing more efficient light bulbs in its buildings and factories.

"That's about enough power for an industrialised city of about seven million people...for a year," said IIEC-Asia associate Peter du Pont, on Wednesday. "In terms of Chinese households, it would be a lot more."
China aims to revamp the country's lighting to make room for cutting investment in power plants and reduce pollutants and greenhouse gas emissions, the IIEC report said.
The saving would be roughly equal to the amount of power produced by five large thermal power plants over the course of a year, the IIEC report said.

The report said the Chinese government would provide up to 100 million Yuan ($12 million) in low interest loans for the lighting industry to upgrade its facilities and produce higher quality energy-efficient bulbs.
The loans would run alongside a nation-wide campaign of education, certification, new policy initiatives, and pilot schemes in government and commercial buildings.
The widespread introduction of compact fluorescent lamps (CFLs) would provide the principal cuts.
"You can screw them (CFLs) into a regular socket... and they basically put out the same amount of light (as a regular bulb) for a quarter of the power," du Pont said.
The report estimated that 250,000 workers were employed in China's 400 or more lamp factories to produce some four billion bulbs a year.

The Beijing Energy Efficiency Center, the analysis wing of the Green Lights program, estimated that 90 percent of these were inefficient and of inferior quality compared to their western counterparts, the report said.
The average CFL produced in China, in the 40-65 lumens per watt range, lasts only 2,000-3,000 hours compared to the international standard of 10,000 hours, the IIEC said.
The poor quality Chinese CFLs are also expensive.
The retail price of a CFL amounts to about 10 percent of the monthly income of the average Chinese family.
Competition and quality would be stimulated by ensuring that only bulbs that met minimum standards for lifetime and efficiency could be certified by the Green Lights program, the IIEC said.
Currently, bulbs that measure up to international standards are exported to earn foreign currency creating a "two-tier" industry.
China recognised the vast scope for cutting back on electricity overproduction following the success of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's own Green Lights program, the study said.
The Chinese program ranks as one of the principal thrusts of the ninth five-year Development Plan (1996-2000), although planning started as far back as 1993, the IIEC said.
China's Green Lights Program Co-ordination Leadership Committee was set up in May last year to gear the work of various state ministries towards streamlining the demand for lighting power.

China has a rapidly expanding market for lamps and lighting equipment, the IIEC said, with sales rising 15 percent per year between 1990-1995 and expected to continue due to government's drive to electrify rural areas.
The IIEC is a non-profit organisation of 60 individuals, founded in 1984, to promote environmentally friendly energy-efficiency policies and technologies the world over.
